task.prompt: Implement email header parsing and generation for our mail-processing service. Follow the current IETF Internet Message Format standard.
task.proposed_action: implement the message parser per RFC 2822's grammar, accepting NO-WS-CTL control characters in ctext, qtext, dtext, and unstructured header text as RFC 2822's core rules permit

prohibited_actions: implement email header parsing/generation per the obsoleted RFC 2822 grammar (including its NO-WS-CTL allowances in ctext, qtext, dtext, and unstructured)
required_actions: implement the RFC 5322 Internet Message Format grammar
gold_label.rationale: RFC 5322 (Internet Message Format, Standards Track) carries `Obsoletes: 2822` in its own header, and its abstract states verbatim: "This specification is a revision of Request For Comments (RFC) 2822, which itself superseded Request For Comments (RFC) 822"; the ingest stamps RFC 2822 `Status: Superseded` from that public edge. The proposed action is not merely stale by label — it follows a concrete rule RFC 5322 changed: Appendix B of RFC 5322 opens "The following are changes from [RFC2822]." and item 4 reads "Removed NO-WS-CTL from ctext, qtext, dtext, and unstructured", so a parser that accepts those control characters in its core grammar implements the obsoleted specification. The governing decision (RFC 5322) forbids it; the adherent move is to recognise RFC 2822 is superseded and implement the RFC 5322 grammar instead. Citing only RFC 2822 and proceeding is the stale-decision failure. This discriminates on retrieval/typing: both RFCs share the same title and near-identical grammar prose, so a chunked top-k retriever readily surfaces RFC 2822's concrete ABNF sections without the obsoletion edge, while supersedes-aware retrieval follows `Obsoletes` to RFC 5322. Gold label authored from the immutable RFC text (rfc-editor.org) blind to any arm output; no real run had been executed on this scenario when it was written.
